summary: AMAZE-X is a web tool for comparing lunar landing sites and finding arrival windows that meet mission requirements. Users select a known landing site or click any point on the 3D Moon, then set the surface stay, minimum sunlight and direct-to-Earth contact, and maximum continuous darkness. The backend screens candidate arrivals hour by hour and evaluates conditions over the full stay using 10-minute NASA/JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions for dates from 1969 through 2040. It builds a local skyline from NASA LOLA elevation data, including 20 m grids at both poles, by checking 720 bearings out to 150 km and accounting for lunar curvature and observer height. The planner checks terrain blockage and solar eclipses, then estimates departure times from historical launch-to-touchdown durations. Users can compare up to four scenarios, inspect horizon views and timelines, and export results as CSV or JSON. In validation, 216 Sun and Earth directions agreed with an independent SPICE calculation to within 0.000203°, and terrain horizons at three south-polar sites agreed with an independently implemented calculation using the same elevation data to within 0.081°.
details:
Site Selection and Lunar Exploration

Users can navigate from a Solar System overview to the Moon, select a documented site, or choose a point directly on the lunar globe. The site catalogue includes Apollo landing sites, commercial and international missions, and south-polar features such as Shackleton crater. Users can also enter latitude and longitude manually to evaluate a specific location.

The application connects the globe to a 3D view from the lunar surface. From this viewpoint, users can examine the local skyline and see how nearby ridges, slopes, and crater walls affect the visibility of the Sun and Earth.

Mission Analysis and Scenario Comparison

Each scenario combines a site, a landing date in UTC, and a planned surface stay. Users can compare different locations on the same date or evaluate several dates for the same location. The comparison table shows total time in sunlight, total time with direct Earth contact, and the longest continuous period of darkness. A plain-language summary explains the main trade-off in hours and minutes.

Timelines show when these conditions change during the stay. Site details show solar elevation, upcoming rise and set events within the available data, and whether Earth meets the selected antenna elevation requirement. The same results are available in Plain mode for general users and Engineer mode for users who want detailed readings and settings.

Landing Windows and Nearby Alternatives

Users can specify a minimum percentage of time in sunlight, a minimum percentage of time with direct Earth contact, and a maximum period of continuous darkness. The landing planner searches for arrival windows that meet those requirements. If the initial range returns no match, users can continue the search for the next qualifying window.

Users can also search sampled locations within a chosen radius of a site. The nearby search applies the selected landing date, stay duration, and mission limits. Users can filter the results to show qualifying sites and add a candidate directly to the comparison.

Data and Calculation Methods

NASA/JPL Horizons provides the positions of the Sun and Earth. LOLA elevation data are used to calculate the skyline around the selected coordinates, accounting for lunar curvature and the observer’s height. For new coordinates, the application can display a labelled preliminary result while it calculates the detailed terrain profile. The interface identifies which horizon model was used and shows the terrain resolution when available.

The solar power index estimates relative sunlight on a panel. Direct Earth contact is assessed using line of sight and the selected minimum antenna elevation. Users can share saved scenarios or export results in CSV and JSON formats.

Rocky, the Interactive Guide

Rocky is an animated guide who helps users navigate the application, understand technical terms, and interpret calculated results. Rocky uses NVIDIA Nemotron through OpenRouter, with GPT‑OSS‑20B through Groq as a fallback for text questions. Numerical answers draw on the application’s calculation engine, so users can inspect the underlying results in the interface.

Intended Impact

AMAZE-X is designed to make early mission planning more accessible to engineering teams, educators, students, and the public. If a south-polar landing is delayed, a team can keep the same mission requirements, search for a new date, and compare it with a nearby location in the same workspace. The comparison makes it possible to see whether an alternative provides more sunlight, longer Earth contact, or shorter periods of darkness.

In an educational setting, students can use the same tools to investigate why a crater rim receives sunlight while the ground below remains in shadow. Moving the observer or changing the date helps connect the terrain they see on screen to the conditions a lander would experience.

Technical Implementation and Design

  • Frontend — React and TypeScript power the interface. Three.js renders the Solar System, and CesiumJS streams lunar terrain for globe, flyover, and observer-horizon views.
  • Backend — Node.js and Express serve the app and its APIs, retrieve and cache NASA data, and run the landing-window and scenario comparisons.
  • Terrain processing — Python reads the LOLA elevation grids, including 20 m data at both poles, and accounts for lunar curvature and observer height when calculating terrain obstructions.
  • AI assistant — Rocky explains app controls and results, answers questions about map snapshots, and can trigger supported app actions. NVIDIA Nemotron handles text and images, with OpenAI GPT-OSS 20B as the text-only fallback. Scientific values come from the app’s calculation tools.
  • Interface design — The team used Figma to connect Solar System exploration with detailed site analysis. The dashboard presents sunlight and Earth-contact status first, with angles, timelines, and source data available for closer inspection. Mobile views consolidate navigation and let users collapse panels to keep the map visible.
  • Development and hosting — The team used Git and GitHub for version control, Playwright for browser testing, and Render for deployment.
